title: Report on Studying Abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to do a three-month clinical clerkship at the Medical University of Gdansk. Now that my study abroad has ended and I am writing this report, I keenly realise once more that my life abroad was supported by a truly large number of people, and I am grateful every day. Presumptuous as it may be, I would like to write this study abroad report.

[What made me want to study abroad] There were mainly two reasons why I wanted to study abroad, neither of them positive or lofty. The first was that I was interested in foreign cultures and life. Although the days were few, through overseas travel I felt on my skin the tremendous energy that local people have for living, and my longing for life abroad grew. The second was that I wanted to break away from a life in a closed space. Because the majority did so, I belonged to a club activity without much thought, neither taking the sport seriously nor achieving results in tournaments, and in a set of values in which drinking large amounts of alcohol and making a ruckus was like a badge of honour, I spent six years somehow as one of many alike within the majority. As the years went by, I came to doubt this way of living. Touching the energy for living that I had felt overseas, I came to feel that I too wanted to live each day with some kind of purpose.

[About the clinical clerkship] Because I am interested in dermatology, I chose departments where skin diseases would be involved: dermatology, tropical medicine, clinical allergology, geriatric medicine and family medicine. I was told that from our year the program had officially been incorporated into the program for local students, and I was allowed to rotate for one to four weeks in each department together with the local students. Also, one must be careful because credit is not given unless one passes the written exam or oral examination on the last day.

The dermatology clerkship consisted of lectures on skin diseases, followed by dividing into groups for surgery observation and medical interviews. Because middle-aged and older patients spoke only Polish, the interviews were done by students who could speak Polish, who translated for us into English, and if we wanted to ask something, we asked through the student who was translating. Because it was the first clinical department I rotated through, for the first few days I was desperately trying to catch the English. Once I had finally got used to listening to English, I then noticed that there was a mountain of knowledge I did not have, and here I came to realise the difference in academic ability from the local students. Also, on the first day of the clerkship we were given 176 pages of teaching material produced by the dermatologists of the Medical University of Gdansk, and since the questions for the written exam on the last day and for the oral examination several weeks after the clerkship came from it, we had to read it thoroughly. Fortunately I passed the exams, but here too I keenly felt that my amount of knowledge and my language ability were clearly inferior to those of the other students. However, fortunately, perhaps because I made the appeal "I want to become a dermatologist" to make up for my lack of academic ability and English, I was given many opportunities to be put in as an assistant during surgery observation. Even after the dermatology clerkship ended, I was also allowed to observe a private clinic on a personal basis.

The tropical medicine clerkship was held at a hospital in Gdynia, rich in nature, about 30 minutes by train from Gdansk, where my dormitory was. In this department I mainly studied parasites such as malaria, echinococcus and Wuchereria bancrofti. There were several patients who said they had been infected while working as missionaries on the African continent, and I realised that Catholic faith is deeply rooted in Poland. It was also impressive that Japanese stationery apparently has an extremely good reputation in other countries, and people wanted the ballpoint pen and eraser I was using.

In the clinical allergology clerkship, I mainly learned about asthma, anaphylactic shock and other allergic diseases. After a lecture for all the students, we received lectures in groups. Rather than talking directly with patients, the clerkship was mainly lectures and actually undergoing tests such as patch tests. The test for this department was an oral examination, and we were asked in great detail about the diagnostic criteria and management of anaphylactic shock.

In the geriatric medicine clerkship, I mainly learned about collagen diseases. Here a very long time was set aside for interviewing patients, and we were asked many questions about the patient's disease, what should be asked in the interview, and complications to be careful of. As I felt in other departments too, I could not hide my surprise that the doctor, without particularly asking permission, suddenly touched the patient's body and gave a lecture to the students. However, the patients did not show displeasure and rather seemed willing to cooperate with us students. I realised that if the country is different, the policy of medical education is different too. Also, when asked in a lecture which country has the highest proportion of elderly population, many students answered Japan, which made me aware that the increase of the elderly population in Japan has become a worldwide problem.

The family medicine clerkship was mainly lectures. A wide range of fields were taken up as subjects, such as how to read an ECG, BMI measurement, body fat percentage measurement, how to examine the chest, pediatric primary care and common psychiatric diseases. According to the supervising instructor, the reason for studying a wide range of fields is that, unlike in Japan, medical instruments such as X-ray and CT are not always available, so one has to accumulate as much knowledge as possible and be able to reach answers from examination results based on that knowledge. Separately from the lectures, there was also a clerkship at a clinic outside the university, and I was allowed to observe at a clinic for children. The diseases were wide-ranging, and it was also a moment when I was convinced by the instructor's words that broad knowledge is necessary. I talked with the doctor at the clinic about the differences in healthcare systems between Poland and Japan, culture and food. There seem to be unexpectedly many people who admire Japan, and he said he would like to go there someday.

[Extracurricular activities] In Poland, extracurricular activities other than the clinical clerkship were also rich, but practising with a professional rugby team, introduced to me by Professor Wozniak, was the most impressive both mentally and physically. I am not an excellent rugby player, but through the kindness of the coach and teammates I was allowed to take part in practice, and was even fortunate to have the opportunity to play as a player in an official rugby sevens match. I was happy just to be able to play rugby at a level far beyond my ability, and I never dreamed I would make many companions who called me a teammate. When they said that they would come to Japan for the Rugby World Cup in Japan in 2019 and asked me to host them, I was so happy I could cry.

[After the study abroad] Looking back, the three months were really short. It is not that my English ability improved dramatically or my medical knowledge increased greatly, and I cannot say for certain that Polish medical care was superior to or more stimulating than Japan's. Compared with me there were many students who were very excellent academically but whose attitude in the clerkship was so bad that it would never be tolerated in Japan. But the students of the Medical University of Gdansk were full of the energy for life that I had once felt, each had dreams and goals for the future and studied toward them, and by talking with them about each other's dreams I was able to recognise that I too have dreams and goals. I also came to feel regret about myself, who had wasted time and so had not achieved much. Through the study abroad I gained many things, such as friends I want to see again, rugby companions and interest in medicine, but above all I strongly feel that I was able to take the first step toward "living each day with a goal."

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and 西尾-san of the International Collaboration Office who made this dispatch possible, to many people including Professor Wozniak of the Medical University of Gdansk, and to my wife, my parents, my wife's family and my friends.
